text: Randolph College is a private liberal arts and sciences college located in Lynchburg, Virginia, United States. It was founded in 1891 as Randolph-Macon Woman's College by William Waugh Smith, then-president of Randolph-Macon College, under Randolph-Macon's charter after he failed to convince R-MC to become coeducational. The college has historic ties to the United Methodist Church and received 50 acres from the city of Lynchburg for its establishment. In 1916, it became the first women's college in the South to earn a Phi Beta Kappa charter. Beginning in 1953, the two colleges were governed by separate boards of trustees. Main Hall, built in 1891, was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979. In August 2006, Randolph-Macon Woman's College announced it would become coeducational and change its name, a decision supported by former Interim president Ginger H. Worden, who argued in a September 17, 2006 editorial for The Washington Post that only 3 percent of college-age women consider women's colleges, and that most applicants were not seeking single-sex education, with seven of the top 10 colleges applicants also being coed. The decision was not universally accepted, with alumnae and students organizing protests covered by local and national media, accusing the administration of recruiting students without informing them of the coeducation plan, and leading to lawsuits. The college was officially renamed Randolph College on July 1, 2007, when it became coeducational. The transition was difficult, with the first full-time male students facing vandalism to mailboxes and doors and experiencing polarization. The last class to receive diplomas from Randolph-Macon Woman's College graduated on May 16, 2010. The college is named after John Randolph of Roanoke, Virginia (1773–1833), an eccentric planter and politician who freed hundreds of slaves in his will and once fought a duel with Henry Clay. Randolph College is primarily an undergraduate institution offering Bachelor of Arts, Bachelor of Science, and Bachelor of Fine Arts degrees in the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences, and also offers Master's programs including a Master of Arts in Teaching, a Master of Fine Arts in Creative Writing, a Master of Fine Arts in Theatre, and a Master of Coaching and Sport Leadership. In the fall of 2021, the college launched a new curriculum model called TAKE2, which divides each semester into seven-week sessions during which students take two courses at a time, differing from the traditional model of taking four or five courses over an entire semester. The Maier Museum of Art, which has been collecting American art since 1920, features works by 19th and 20th-century American artists and houses several thousand paintings, prints, drawings, and photographs in its permanent collection. The museum hosts special exhibitions and education programs annually. In 2007, the college faced controversy when it announced it would sell four paintings from its collection. The college has a tradition of rivalry between 'odd' and 'even' graduating classes, based on whether their graduation year is odd or even, resulting in two odd and two even 'sister-classes' that participate in shared events. Since 1968, the college has hosted a study abroad program at the University of Reading, England, selecting up to 35 students each year, commonly during the junior year, who may enroll for the full academic year or for a semester, living in one of three Randolph-owned houses near the campus and traveling together to various cities in England. In 2018, the Randolph College Board of Trustees decided to end the World in Britain program after the following academic year. A minor in American Culture allows students to study American society and culture through interdisciplinary approaches and also accepts visiting students from other U.S. colleges for a one-semester intensive study of themes or regions, including literature, art, history, and travel. Randolph College is affiliated with NCAA Division III and competes in the Old Dominion Athletic Conference (ODAC), offering intercollegiate sports in nine varsity disciplines: basketball, cross country, lacrosse, soccer, swimming, tennis, track and field, volleyball, and wrestling. The college fields six men's and eight women's varsity teams.
